claims.text: Creep resistance in FCC/BCC HEA protective coatings is governed by sluggish diffusion arising from severe lattice distortion and multi-element disorder.
Sluggish diffusion impedes dislocation climb during continuous high-temperature loading.
Sluggish diffusion impedes grain-boundary migration during continuous high-temperature loading.
Impeded dislocation climb and grain-boundary migration reduce progressive plastic deformation.
The starting HEA coating has a homogeneous microstructure and minimal pre-existing defects.
Sustained mechanical stress at elevated temperature induces creep deformation.
Thermally activated creep is expected in an approximate temperature range of 0.4–0.7 Tm.
A controlled atmosphere prevents oxidation during the creep experiment.
Severe lattice distortion and multi-element disorder are characteristic structural features of HEAs.
Severe lattice distortion and multi-element disorder reduce atomic mobility.
Atomic diffusion is necessary for dislocation climb and grain-boundary migration during creep.
The HEA coating will have a significantly lower steady-state creep rate than conventional single-element or binary FCC/BCC alloys under identical loading and temperature.
The HEA coating will take longer than conventional single-element or binary FCC/BCC alloys to reach an equivalent strain.
The creep-resistance effect persists while the microstructure remains stable and phase separation and catastrophic grain-boundary failure do not occur.
Very high temperature or extreme stress can overcome the sluggish-diffusion effect.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction varies with HEA composition, grain size, and processing history.

contradictions.description: The prediction requires a significantly lower creep rate, but the falsification rule rejects the hypothesis only when there is no lower rate at all. A small or statistically insignificant decrease would therefore fail the stated prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
